running after it had finished. Closing idle connections wasn't enough: a browser

Add a configurable volume step size to the players core config (#5571)

The four volume nudge commands (`cmd_volume_up`/`_down` and their group
equivalents) each hardcoded the same adaptive ladder: step 1 below 10 or
above 90, step 2 below 30 or above 70, step 3 in the middle. That ladder
now lives behind a single `_get_volume_step` helper, and a new
`volume_step` integer entry on the `players` core config overrides it
with a flat step.

`0` is the default and means "keep the adaptive ladder", so behaviour on
existing installs is unchanged. The value is read per command rather
than cached, so a change takes effect without a reload.

At the request of maintainers, putting the setting on the server rather
than in a front-end UI makes it apply consistently everywhere: the
scroll wheel and tap-at-the-edges already call
`players/cmd/volume_up`/`volume_down`, so they have always followed the
server ladder, and a frontend-only setting could never reach them.

fix(tree): expand subtree reaches every descendant

"Expand subtree" walked down only through branches that were already
expanded, so collapsed descendants were never reached and the command
in effect opened a single level. "Collapse subtree" had the mirror
image: expanded notes below a collapsed one stayed expanded and
reappeared opened when that note was expanded again.

The recursive query now walks the whole subtree and filters on
`isExpanded` only in the final SELECT, returning just the branches
whose state has to change. It keeps `UNION` over `(branchId, noteId)`,
so a note cloned under two parents contributes its children once.

The specs build a subtree with an already-expanded child, a collapsed
grandchild and a converging clone; both fail on the previous query
(expand returned 2 of 8 branches, collapse 6 of 8) and pass under the
server and standalone suites.

Supersedes #8525, whose depth-limited query skipped the subtree below
an already-expanded child and returned clone descendants twice.

GEQtools: fix bcentr inflation from x-point in to_profiles R0

MITIMgeqdsk.to_profiles set the reference major radius from the global (max,min) of R over the separatrix, so for diverted equilibria min(R) was the x-point (large |Z|, small R), not the inboard midplane. That shrank R0 and inflated the vacuum field B0 = (R*Bt)/R0 written to bcentr (e.g. R0 1.587 -> bcentr 2.118 T instead of 1.68 -> 2.0 T at nominal Bt=2.0 T). Compute R0 from the boundary crossings at the magnetic-axis elevation instead; this avoids the off-midplane x-point and reduces to (max+min)/2 for limited/circular boundaries.

Add binary-search debug protocol for iris checksum mismatches (#2039)

* Add binary-search debug protocol for iris checksum mismatches

When the 3-party state check detects differing iris checksums, a new
debug protocol kicks in to identify the exact serial IDs that differ.

Uses prefix sums over SetHash (which is additive) so any range hash is
O(1), then binary-searches the serial-ID space: each round splits open
ranges at the midpoint, exchanges left-half hashes via VecRing64, and
recurses into whichever half(s) still disagree. Finds up to 64 differing
serial IDs in O(log N) network rounds carrying O(K) values each.

The core algorithm is extracted into a networking-free IrisDiffSearch
state machine, tested with 8 scenarios simulating 3 parties locally.

fix(ai-chat): correct silent data errors in the observability tool belt

Five confirmed correctness bugs where a tool quietly returned wrong or partial
data — the worst failure mode for an assistant that's supposed to be trusted.

1. query_metrics scanned full retention. The aggregate query carried no time
   predicate; startTimestamp/endTimestamp only shape the bucket grid, so
   percentiles/aggregates mixed in data from outside the requested window. Add
   an explicit `time` InBetween filter to the query (MetricTools).

2. log_histogram dropped the most recent buckets. getHistogram returns one row
   per (bucket, severity); with ~60 buckets and 2+ severities that exceeded the
   serializer's 50-row cap, which kept the OLDEST 50 and discarded the newest —
   so spike detection missed recent spikes. Pivot to one row per time bucket
   (severities as fields) and bound the bucket count, so every bucket survives
   and the output is more compact (LogTools).

3. get_trace silently truncated at 100 spans and rendered orphaned subtrees as
   roots. Raise the limit and, when hit, append an explicit truncation note and
   flag isTruncated instead of pretending the trace was complete (TraceTools).

4. getTimeRange swallowed bad timestamps. A non-ISO startTime/endTime was
   silently ignored and the default window used, answering a different question.
   Throw BadDataException so the model self-corrects with a valid value
   (ToolTypes).

5. Row-cap truncation was invisible to the model. serializeRows capped at 50 and
   set isTruncated but added no marker to the text, so the model reported a slice
   as the whole picture. Append a "showing the first 50 of N rows" marker
   (Serializer).

Tests: getTimeRange validation/clamp suite; serializer truncation-marker cases.
Common typecheck clean; all 44 AI tests pass; ESLint clean.

A save's preprocessor run goes ahead of the checks waiting

The preprocessor's one worker took work in the order it came, so a save
waited behind every check queued before it, and a check for text typed
over since still ran in full. Work is now handed to the worker one piece
at a time from two lanes: runs, which a save waits on, first, then the
analyzers' expansions. A check still waiting when the same script is
asked to be checked again is not made at all; the later one answers
both, the earlier's caller seeing a newer text than it asked about, as
the studio already expects.

PERF022 + push_from / push_clone_from / emplace_from bulk overloads

Adds unambiguous bulk-append names mirroring push/push_clone/emplace,
backfills the existing bulk forms with reserve() so they stop paying
N reallocations, and ships a lint rule (PERF022) that flags the
hand-rolled for-loop element-at-a-time shape and recommends the
new _from name.

The single names push/push_clone are overloaded between single-
element and bulk forms - B |> push(arr) silently flips meaning
depending on whether B is array of T or array of T-array. The _from
suffix names the bulk intent unambiguously.

PERF022 details:
  - Fires on for (s in A) { B |> push(s) } and push_clone, all
    three pipe/dot/plain-call shapes (compiler folds to the same
    ExprCall).
  - Body must be exactly one statement; if-guarded, multi-stmt,
    transform-then-push, multi-source, and nested for-loop shapes
    do NOT match (no clean bulk migration).
  - Source must be array of T or C-array - range/string/iterator/
    generator sources have no bulk overload.
  - Destination must be array of T - generic auto destinations
    (e.g. [expect_any_vector] clone(args, ...) in builtin.das)
    are skipped because push_from doesn't exist for dasvector.
  - Warns at the for-loop's .at (not the inner push's) so the
    same-location dedup in perf_warning doesn't collide with
    PERF006 which fires at the push.
  - emplace is out of scope: for-iter-var is const-ref, but
    emplace requires var-ref, so the hand-rolled shape doesn't
    compile in the first place.

builtin.das additions (11 new overloads): push_from x4,
push_clone_from x4 (fills the array of numT source gap that
push_clone didn't have), emplace_from x3 (gap-fill too). Each calls
reserve(long_length(Arr) + long_length(varr)) before iterating.

Existing bulk push/push_clone/emplace overloads also get the
reserve() backfill so the old name stays efficient for callers
that don't migrate. array-of-arrays single-element overloads
(push(array of T-array, T-array)) are out of scope - those push a
sub-array as ONE element, not bulk.

CODAP-1290: case card and formula observer reactivity (#2556)

* CODAP-1290: refresh case card values on external changes

The case card uses MobX observers to display values, but the per-element
accessors (attr.strValue/value/numValue) read volatile arrays whose
element mutations are not deeply observable; only the existing length
and type views track attr.changeCount. Touching changeCount in the two
case card consumer paths makes the observer fire on value mutations
without imposing tracking overhead on hot graph/map/collection paths
that share those accessors.

- summarizedValues view tracks attr.changeCount so summary cells
  re-evaluate when any value in the attribute mutates.
- CaseAttrView observer tracks attr?.changeCount so per-case rows
  re-render when their case's value changes.

Adds unit tests covering numeric and categorical summary reactivity.

* CODAP-1290: refresh formula observers when canonical form changes

When a formula referenced a symbol (e.g. a slider's global value) by
name before that symbol existed, the formula's static dependency list
was captured empty at registration time. Adding the symbol later
correctly updated the canonical form and triggered a one-shot
recalculation, but the dependency-keyed observers (observeGlobalValues
in particular) were not refreshed, so subsequent value changes on the
newly-resolved symbol were silently missed.

In setupFormulaObservers' updateDisplay closure, when the canonical
form changes, dispose and re-register the formula's observers so the
new dependency set is tracked.

Adds a focused regression test that creates a formula referencing a
slider name before the slider exists, adds the slider, and asserts
subsequent value changes trigger recalculation.

The time zone converter reaches typed members only

Registered on the serializer, a converter is consulted for a value's runtime
type wherever that value appears - including a TimeZoneInfo held as an object in
a job data map, which it wrote as a bare string, dropping the $type that path
carries. QuartzContractResolver now attaches it per property, to members typed
as a TimeZoneInfo, and it is out of the converter list. That still reaches every
trigger's TimeZone, which is the whole of #3494, and leaves object-typed slots
byte for byte as they were.

Captured rather than assumed, both times. A job data map holding a zone writes
the same bytes at 347392bd and here, $type and read-only properties and all, and
NewtonsoftJobDataTimeZoneTest asserts that payload verbatim.

That payload has never been readable back: IgnoreSerializableInterface keeps
Json.NET off TimeZoneInfo's ISerializable implementation, so it writes public
members that are all read-only and has nothing to construct a zone from on the
way in. Writing $type explicitly does not help either - with the slot declared
as object, Json.NET resolves the type name and then goes down the object-contract
path rather than dispatching to the converter. So the round trip being asked
about here cannot be made to work by a converter, was not working before, and is
recorded as the limitation it is rather than quietly repaired or quietly lost.

The refusal from #3495 lives in JobDataMapConverter, which AddQuartzConverters
registers for the HTTP API as well as the store, so it reaches a job data map on
its way into a response too. That is the consistent outcome - the client reads
with this same closed reader - but the message said "a persistent store cannot
read back", which is not what a caller of the HTTP API is looking at. It now says
"Quartz's JSON format", and the way out it names was already right for both.

fix: CFF primitive reader stale outValue (V-043/V-050) (#361)

Every CFFPrimitiveReader::Read* (ReadByte, ReadCard16, Read{3,4}ByteUnsigned
plus their signed/wrapper variants and ReadOffset) used to return eFailure
without writing outValue when the underlying stream was exhausted or the
reader was already in sticky-failure state. Callers in
CFFFileInput::ReadEncoding / ReadFDSelect deliberately discard the per-call
status (V-050) and feed the locals straight into heap allocations and
mFDArray / mFDSelect indexing — partial garbage on a truncated CFF.

Initialize outValue at function entry across the named primitives so
failure paths now consistently leave outValue == 0. Same shape as PR #360
for the OpenType reader.

V-050's underlying concern — "partial garbage drives heap-corrupting
paths before failure surfaces" — is closed structurally by this contract:
fdIndex / nextRangeGlyphIndex / encoding-loop counts are now
deterministically zero once the reader has failed, so the ignored-status
loops in ReadEncoding / ReadFDSelect can no longer drive sized allocations
or array indexing off attacker-influenced stale values. Refactoring those
two callers to capture statuses explicitly is the alternative listed in
the C1 cluster spec ("OR callers always check GetInternalState() between
reads"); the init-at-source approach taken here matches the rest of the
cluster and lands a much smaller diff.

arch: riscv: add soc hook to close the syscall ecall

Some RISC-V SoCs cannot deliver a fault raised by the syscall
body itself while the ECALL exception of a user-mode syscall is
still being handled. The stack guard below the privileged stack
catches a syscall whose call chain runs too deep, but on such a
SoC that access fault is reported asynchronously inside the open
ECALL and locks the core up, resetting the chip with nothing
delivered to software. A user-mode application can therefore
reset the board through the depth of a granted service call.

Masking interrupts does not help here. The existing
RISCV_SOC_HAS_SYSCALL_INTMASK holds off the interrupt
controller, while this fault comes from the body itself.

Add the hidden RISCV_SOC_SYSCALL_CLOSE_ECALL option. When a SoC
selects it, the IRQ wrapper leaves the exception before running
the syscall body: it returns to the following instruction with
the previous privilege set to machine mode, so the body runs on
the same privileged stack with the same privileges but outside
the exception. A fault taken there is an ordinary top-level trap
the SoC delivers normally, and a syscall that overflows the
privileged stack is reported as a stack overflow that kills only
the offending thread.

The exception exit path reloads the exception program counter
and status register from the saved frame, so borrowing both here
does not disturb the return to user mode.

Make the SQLite durable dequeue actually write the inbox row

SqliteQueue implements IDatabaseBackedEndpoint, which tells DurableReceiver that
the transport has already persisted the incoming envelope and to skip its own
inbox INSERT. SqliteQueueListener did not keep that promise: it dequeued as
SELECT -> DELETE -> COMMIT -> hand to the receiver, with no incoming-envelope
insert anywhere in that transaction.

So a durable SQLite queue had a committed state in which the queue row was gone,
no inbox row existed, and the only copy of the message was in memory inside a
running handler. Killing the process there lost the message outright -- it was in
neither the queue nor the inbox.

The durable pop now moves the selected rows out of the queue table and into the
message store's incoming-envelope table in ONE transaction, and commits before
the envelopes are exposed to the receiver -- the same invariant the PostgreSQL and
SQL Server durable pops hold. The buffered path keeps the destructive dequeue it
has always had; a BufferedInMemory listener does not pay for durability it did
not ask for.

No schema change: the existing incoming-envelope table is the destination.

Details worth knowing, since SQLite is not PostgreSQL here:

- Write concurrency. Microsoft.Data.Sqlite's BeginTransaction defaults to
  deferred: false, i.e. BEGIN IMMEDIATE, so the database-wide write lock is taken
  at BEGIN rather than at the first write. That is what makes the combined
  SELECT + DELETE + INSERT safe: a DEFERRED transaction that reads and then
  writes must upgrade its lock, and SQLite answers a contended upgrade with a
  SQLITE_BUSY that no busy_timeout can wait out. At BEGIN the busy handler does
  apply, so concurrent listeners serialize (SqliteConnection.DefaultTimeout, 30s)
  and a genuine timeout surfaces as the existing backoff-and-retry with every
  queue row still in place. There is no ctid/FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED equivalent
  and, with one writer at a time, none is needed.

- Idempotency. The inbox row is written status = 'Incoming' and owner_id = this
  node's assigned number, as the other two do. The recovery sweep only reclaims
  owner_id = 0, so the local listener and the sweep cannot both claim it.

- Id rendering. The queue tables store ids as lower-case "D" text (the sender
  binds a string) while the inbox stores what Microsoft.Data.Sqlite renders a
  Guid parameter as, which is UPPER case. So the insert goes through the store's
  own DatabasePersistence command rather than an `insert ... select id from
  queue`, which would have written rows that mark-as-handled could never retire.

- The anti-duplicate guard PostgreSQL and SQL Server run as a pre-delete is kept,
  but probed against the batch's own ids instead of every inbox row for the
  address: on SQLite that probe runs inside a lock over the whole database file,
  so it is a primary-key lookup bounded by MaximumMessagesToReceive rather than a
  scan. Same reasoning as the bounded reaps in SqliteMessageStore (GH-4567).

Fixes #4758

Fix Edit Mode mouse interaction broken when game is embedded in Glue (#2183) (#2184)

IsGameOrGlueActive (via IsParentGlueFocused) required GetForegroundWindow() to exactly match Glue's own MainWindowHandle, but the embedded game window is reparented via a raw SetParent with no WS_CHILD style fixup, so Windows still lets it take OS foreground/activation on its own when clicked. GetForegroundWindow() then returns the game's own window, not Glue's, so the gate was closed almost the entire time a user was actually using the embedded panel - silently breaking click-select, deselect, and middle-mouse camera pan. The old '|| Game.IsActive' fallback (removed by #2158's fix for #2154) had masked this for years.

Treat OS foreground being owned by the embedded game's own process as equivalent to Glue being focused - that's exactly the state while a user is legitimately interacting with the embedded panel, and it still correctly blocks the #2154 case (an unrelated window truly covering everything).

TML-2928: PSL formatter — CST-based pretty-printer + prisma format CLI (#850)

## What

Delivers the **PSL formatter** for Prisma Next, end to end: a
deterministic pretty-printer engine plus the `prisma format` CLI command
that runs it.

**1. Engine** — `@prisma-next/psl-parser/format`:

```ts
import { format, type FormatOptions, PslFormatError } from '@prisma-next/psl-parser/format';

format(source);                                  // canonical PSL, LF, 2-space indent
format(source, { indent: 'tab', newline: 'CRLF' });
```

`format(source, options?) -> string` parses via the CST and re-emits
canonical PSL. Pure string→string: no file I/O, no node built-ins, no
`@prisma-next/config` dependency.

**2. CLI** — `prisma format`:

Reads `prisma-next.config.ts`; when the contract source is PSL
(`config.contract.source.sourceFormat === 'psl'`), formats
`config.contract.source.inputs[0]` **in place**. Non-PSL or absent
sources are left untouched. Indent/newline come from an optional
`formatter` config section; the system newline (`os.EOL`) is resolved at
the CLI.

Closes TML-2928 (the whole issue — both the engine and the CLI).

## Why

Prisma Next authors hand-write and machine-emit PSL, but there was no
canonical formatter for the new authoring stack. The new red/green CST
preserves all trivia (whitespace, comments, newlines) as tokens, making
it the right substrate for a lossless pretty-printer: re-emit a
normalized, deterministic layout while retaining comments and the full
token stream.

## Engine behaviour

- **CST-based** (`parse` + typed AST wrappers); does not touch the
legacy `parsePslDocument`.
- **`indent`**: positive integer (spaces) or `'tab'`; default 2.
- **`newline`**: `'LF'` (default) or `'CRLF'`, applied uniformly.
- **Per-block alignment**: field-name→type column and trailing
attributes aligned per block.
- **Trivia preservation**: leading / trailing / dangling comments and
author blank lines (collapsed to one, never adjacent to a brace).
- **Blank line before block attributes**: one blank line always
separates the last field from the first `@@` attribute (house style).
- **Idempotence**: `format(format(x)) === format(x)`.
- **Refuses** input that carries parse diagnostics (`PslFormatError`)
rather than emitting best-effort output.

## Key decisions

- **Engine ships inside `@prisma-next/psl-parser`** via a `./format`
subpath — no separate package, no new runtime dependency. Engine option
validation is hand-rolled (the option space is two enum-ish fields; a
schema lib would have violated the package's no-new-deps constraint).
The `formatter` **config** section, by contrast, is arktype-validated —
`@prisma-next/config` already depends on arktype.
- **`os.EOL` resolution lives only in the CLI.** The engine never reads
`os`; the `prisma format` command resolves `config.formatter.newline ??
(os.EOL === '\r\n' ? 'CRLF' : 'LF')` and passes an explicit `newline`
into the engine.
- **PSL-ness is a structured discriminator, not a filename heuristic.**
`ContractSourceProvider` carries an optional `sourceFormat: 'psl' |
'typescript'`; every first-party provider declares it
(`prismaContract`/`mongoContract` → `'psl'`; the `typescript*`/`empty`
helpers → `'typescript'`). The command formats only `'psl'` sources;
anything else (incl. absent) is left untouched.
- **Inline `//` comments are a hard break barrier.** `field Type
//comment` followed by a continuation `@attribute` preserves the break
rather than hoisting the attribute past the comment — matching Prettier,
Biome, and rustfmt (a `//` comment runs to end-of-line; joining a later
token onto its line is both a correctness and an idempotence hazard).

## Tests — side-by-side fixture pairs

The formatter's integration oracle is a set of hand-authored
**side-by-side pairs** under
`test/format/fixtures/<case>/{input,expected}.prisma` — open a pair to
*see* exactly what the formatter does. The test asserts `format(input)
=== expected`, idempotence, and that formatting actually happened. Cases
cover alignment, comment preservation, the inline-comment hard break,
blank-line handling, block-attribute spacing, enum/generic blocks, and
the namespaced-type round-trip (`space:ns.Type`). The CLI is covered by
an e2e journey (`format.e2e.test.ts`) proving format-in-place,
leave-untouched, and refuse-on-unparseable, each asserting on-disk file
state.

## Validation

- `pnpm lint:deps` — no violations (engine takes no node built-ins; the
CLI→engine edge is layering-safe).
- `@prisma-next/psl-parser` — 529 tests, no type errors; fixture pairs
produce no snapshot churn.
- `@prisma-next/config` — 29 tests (discriminator + `formatter`
section).
- `@prisma-next/cli` — `prisma format` operation tests + the e2e journey
green. (Note: ~9 pre-existing flakes in `version.test.ts` /
`removed-verb-redirects.test.ts` are cold-boot subprocess-timeout
fragility, unrelated to this work.)

## Base

Targets `main`. The formatter consumes the fault-tolerant CST parser
surface, which landed on `main` via #795 and #849; this branch was
originally stacked on the pre-merge `psl-cst-parser` branch and has been
rebased onto `main` now that the CST work is merged.

Fix file locking on 32-bit GNU/Linux

The locking protocol reserves bytes near 2^62, but libc::off_t is only
32 bits on targets such as i686-unknown-linux-gnu. Converting lock offsets
or lengths to off_t panics, including during ordinary database opens.

Use flock64 on GNU/Linux and route acquisitions, queries, and unlocks
through the appropriate large-file fcntl syscall. This avoids glibc's
narrow flock conversion without requiring the fcntl64 symbol introduced
in glibc 2.28.

Add regressions for distinct high and low offsets, large range boundaries,
and blocking locks. Run the locking tests with default and all features,
and the multi-process integration tests, on i686 in CI.

Fix a regression introduced in 30.1.0 when focusing an element after removing the previously focused element. Removal leaves the document's viewport focused, represented internally by the Document. Treating that sentinel as the previous element caused spurious window blur and focusout events and exposed the Document as relatedTarget. Use focus chains and remove their common trailing entries so this transition fires only focus and focusin, with a null relatedTarget.

Implement shared focusing, unfocusing, and focus-update steps. Resolve non-focusable document elements to their viewports, redirect iframe targets to their content documents, and track focus transitions through ancestor documents. Unfocusing checks chain membership and current focusability before focusing the top-level viewport.

Recheck focusability before designating each new focused area, so targets removed or disabled by blur listeners do not become active. Apply selection changes before focus dispatch and stop clearing selection after blur, preserving selections established by event listeners.

Preserve the interoperable behavior of clearing old focus before blur dispatch and honoring focus changes made by blur listeners. These gaps in the written algorithm are tracked by https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/1569 and https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/12329. Follow the specified viewport resolution and top-level unfocusing behavior where browsers differ.

Document unsupported steps, including inertness, shadow-root focus delegation, rendering, and system focus. Documents continue to represent their viewports; asynchronous focus fixup remains separate.

Refactor MFEM executed objects off user objects

Move MFEM initial conditions, aux kernels, submesh transfers, postprocessors, and vector
postprocessors onto a shared MFEMExecutedObject base backed directly by MooseObject instead of the
libMesh/MOOSE user-object stack.

This introduces an MFEM-owned executed-object scheduling path in MFEMProblem. Executed MFEM objects
are now collected from the warehouse by MFEM-specific system name, dependency ordered from the
resources they produce and consume, and then initialized/executed/finalized explicitly. Variable,
postprocessor, and vector-postprocessor dependencies now provide the ordering signal that used to be
expressed through execution_order_group.

As part of that split, MFEMGeneralUserObject is removed entirely. The executed MFEM families no
longer inherit GeneralUserObject machinery, and the MFEM docs and test inputs are updated to reflect
the new dependency-driven model rather than user-object execution groups.

The refactor also adapts the framework touch points that previously assumed MFEM PP/VPP objects were
user objects. AdvancedOutput now discovers MFEM postprocessors and vector postprocessors from their
own warehouse systems, FEProblemBase and VectorPostprocessorInterface can resolve MFEM vector
postprocessors by PPName(), and MFEMProblem finalizes MFEM PP/VPP reporter data in its explicit
execution pass.

Non-MFEM postprocessors and vector postprocessors in an MFEMProblem still go through the normal
framework add path, while MFEM-native PP/VPP objects use the new MFEM executed-object machinery.

Skip empty directories in uv build outputs (#19437)

## Summary

This updates the uv build backend so wheels and source distributions no
longer emit standalone empty directory entries. Directory entries are
still written when they are ancestors of included files, preserving the
existing deterministic archive structure for real package content.

## Root cause

The build walkers wrote directory entries as they encountered matching
directories. That meant empty directories, and directories whose
contents were excluded later, could appear in build outputs even though
they contained no installable or source content.

## Changes

- Collect included file paths and their ancestor directories before
writing archive entries.
- Skip raw directory entries that do not have included descendants.
- Preserve deterministic output order with `BTreeMap` collection before
writing.
- Extend the build-backend snapshot fixture with an empty directory and
an excluded `__pycache__` directory so the regression is covered for
both sdists and wheels.

- `cargo test -p uv-build-backend built_by_uv_building`
- `cargo test -p uv-build-backend`

warnings`

* electroMechanicalLaw: field-based Ta and own fibre tensors (#237)

Extend electroMechanicalLaw to support field-based active tension (Ta)
and to own the fibre structural tensors (f0f0, f0f0f) by reading them
from the f0/f0f fields at construction time.

Changes:
- electroMechanicalLaw: add f0f0_ and f0f0f_ volSymmTensorField members,
  constructed from f0 and f0f fields in 0/solid/. The law no longer
  looks up "f0f0"/"f0f0f" in the objectRegistry (which required
  GuccioneElastic to be the passive law). Now any passive law can be
  used.
- electroMechanicalLaw: lazy field-based Ta check using fieldTaChecked_
  and useFieldTa_ flags. On the first correct() call, the law checks
  for a "Ta" volScalarField in the objectRegistry. If found, it is used
  for active tension instead of the constant Ta_ + ramp logic. This
  allows external coupling models (e.g. sequentialElectroMechanical in
  cardiacFoam) to register a Ta field and drive the active tension.
  Fully backwards-compatible: if no Ta field is registered, the original
  constant-Ta + ramp behaviour is preserved.
- solidModel: add virtual couplingField(const word&) method returning
  a tmp<volTensorField>, for future mechano-electric feedback (e.g.
  fibre stretch passed back to the electro model).

These changes are designed to support the electro-mechanical coupling
framework in cardiacFoam (https://github.com/cardiacFoam/cardiacFoam),
where the sequentialElectroMechanical coupling model registers a Ta
field on the solid mesh each time step after extracting Ca_i from the
ionic model.

the case continues to pass on the versions the reference was generated

* Add an optional unity build for libsolids4FoamModels (#300)

* Add an optional unity build for libsolids4FoamModels

Compiling each of the library's ~230 sources separately means the large
set of OpenFOAM headers is re-parsed once per source, and that parsing,
rather than the solids4foam code itself, dominates the build time.

Setting S4F_UNITY_BUILD=1 groups the sources into buckets, where each
bucket is a generated source file which #includes the sources assigned to
it, so the headers are parsed once per bucket. A from-scratch build of
the library with -j 16 drops from 119 s to 41 s, a speed-up of about 2.9.
The library produced is unchanged, and the build is conventional unless
the variable is set.

Make/makeUnityFiles generates the buckets from the canonical source list,
which remains the single point of maintenance: new classes are added to
Make/files.openfoam or Make/files.foamextend as before. Sources which
cannot share a translation unit with their neighbours can be listed in
Make/unity-exclude and are then compiled on their own. The macros in
eig3.C are #undef'ined so that they do not leak into the rest of a
bucket.

The library builds from scratch as a unity build on OpenFOAM-v2512,
OpenFOAM-9 and foam-extend-4.1, and switching back to a conventional
build works in each case. On OpenFOAM-v2512, the plateHole tutorial run
against the unity-built library converges and agrees with the analytical
solution as before.

* Fix PETSc Jacobian preallocation (#309)

* Fix PETSc Jacobian preallocation by using a block AIJ matrix

initialiseJacobian created the Jacobian as MATMPIAIJ but preallocated it
with MatMPIBAIJSetPreallocation. That function dispatches via
PetscTryMethod, so it silently does nothing for a MATMPIAIJ matrix: the
computed d_nnz and o_nnz were discarded and the matrix was never
preallocated. Verified by removing the preallocation call entirely, which
gave byte-identical results.

PETSc-3.19 changed MatCheckPreallocated to call MatSetUp when a matrix is
not preallocated, and switched unpreallocated AIJ matrices to hash-table
assembly, which hid the problem. Older versions do not:

  - PETSc <= 3.18 with --with-debugging=1 fails in SNESSetFromOptions with
    "Must call MatXXXSetPreallocation(), MatSetUp() ...", reached via
    PCGetDefaultType_Private -> MatGetFactorAvailable.
  - PETSc <= 3.18 with --with-debugging=0 compiles MatCheckPreallocated to
    nothing, so PETSc uses an un-preallocated matrix and segfaults. This is
    the crash reported in #279, where PETSc came from the Ubuntu packages.

Create the matrix as MATMPIBAIJ so the existing block preallocation
applies. This also restores the intended preallocation on newer PETSc,
which was silently falling back to dynamic assembly.

Verified with the wobblyNewton tutorial and OpenFOAM-v2512:

  - PETSc 3.18.6 (debug): previously fatal, now runs to completion.
  - PETSc 3.24.0: no regression, type mpibaij, bs 3, 755919 nonzeros,
    allocated exactly, zero mallocs during MatSetValues.

* Preallocate the Jacobian with MatXAIJSetPreallocation

Creating the Jacobian as MATMPIBAIJ fixed the preallocation but broke
PCFIELDSPLIT: the decayingTaylorGreenVortex case splits inside a bs=3
block (pc_fieldsplit_0_fields "0,1", pc_fieldsplit_1_fields "2"), and
PETSc cannot extract sub-matrices that cut across BAIJ blocks:

    Cannot use MATBAIJ with PCFIELDSPLIT and currently set matrix and
    PC blocksizes
      #1 PCSetUp_FieldSplit()

Instead, keep the matrix as MATMPIAIJ and preallocate it with
MatXAIJSetPreallocation, which takes the same per-block-row counts but
dispatches on the type the matrix actually has, rather than silently
doing nothing as the type-specific routines do. This preallocates the
matrix for AIJ, BAIJ and SBAIJ alike, so it also survives a user
-mat_type override.

Verified with OpenFOAM-v2512 and PETSc 3.24: decayingTaylorGreenVortex
passes its regression test, and wobblyNewton runs to completion with
MAT_NEW_NONZERO_ALLOCATION_ERR set. Deliberately shrinking d_nnz by one
makes the latter fail with "New nonzero caused a malloc" in
MatSetValues_MPIAIJ, confirming the preallocation reaches the matrix and
that the counts are exact.

  against the undeformed face normal, which is only correct for linear
  geometry.

  bulkModulus(). Quadrature-point stress evaluation was previously only
  available in linearElastic; the other finite strain laws continue to
  report the existing notImplemented error.

  required.

  is the traction per unit area in the configuration at the start of the
  time step. This is integrated against the current mesh magSf.

feat: publish StorageV3 index artifacts through segment manifests (#53048)

Publishes completed StorageV3 index artifacts through the segment
manifest while
keeping build-task state durable until publication. Builds on the
segment-scoped
manifest commit framework from #52621.

## What changes

**Publication and placement.**
`dataCoord.index.writeSegmentIndexToManifest`
(default `false`) controls new completed artifacts. When enabled, a
Finished
StorageV3 build with files publishes its manifest entry and advances the
segment
pointer while deleting its etcd task row in one catalog transaction; its
index
record remains available in memory. Unissued, InProgress, Failed,
fake-Finished,
and StorageV1/V2 records continue to persist in etcd. Disabling the
switch directs
new completions to etcd without hiding already published manifest
indexes.

**Recovery.** The per-segment `manifest_has_index` marker determines
which retained
healthy or Dropped non-L0 StorageV3 manifests are read, independently of
the current
write mode. Existing etcd records win BuildID conflicts. Recovered
records also
retain indexes belonging to dropped definitions so GC can find their
artifacts.
Dropped compaction parents recover their indexes for query fallback and
orphan-GC
protection. Unreadable or invalid marked manifests fail startup, except
when a
separate successful existence check proves a Dropped segment's manifest
was
already removed by GC. That exception leaves the marker intact for
pending GC.
Confirmed empty sections normalize historical true markers against the
exact
published pointer.

Manifest reads share one metadata-owner admission budget across
recovery, copy
assembly, copy verification and GC.
`segmentIndexManifestLoadConcurrency` defaults
to 64, is clamped to 1–256, and is capped by positive
`minio.maxConnections` values.
Startup uses fixed-size batches and per-segment retries; an exhausted
read does
not replay the entire scan through the metastore retry loop.

**Retirement and synchronization.** GC deletes unused index bytes before
removing
their manifest entries and records, retaining the metadata needed to
retry failed
deletion. It refreshes segment placement after admitting terminal index
tasks so
a concurrently completed publication is not classified using an older
marker or
revision. The commit lock order is
`segmentManifestLocks -> indexMeta.keyLock -> segMu`. BuildID locks span
the initial
snapshot, manifest I/O and publication; `segMu` is released during
object-storage
I/O. OVERWRITE applies updates to the explicitly selected input
revision; higher
stored revisions affect version allocation, not the input contents.

**Copy and restore.** Dispatch persists the selected index placement and
sends
target index identities keyed by name. Capable workers receive shared
request-level
definitions; older workers receive the per-target encoding. The worker
removes
inherited source entries and republishes the copied target artifacts.
DataCoord
validates artifact-bearing manifests before publishing any target,
including
identity, parameters, path layout and file keys. V1/V2 target indexes
remain in
etcd even when the task selected manifest placement for its V3 siblings.

Coordinator-derived cleanup prefixes are persisted before dispatch for
every
storage version, including each retry's allocated index directories.
Rejected
completed results retain durable cleanup intent. A separate cleanup
worker waits
for ordinary segment GC to retire every target, preserving its snapshot,
loaded-reader, pause and retention protections, then removes leftover
task-owned
prefixes. A per-task lock excludes cleanup from result installation.
Failed tasks
with cleanup plans reject late completions; failed admission writes and
restart
retain polling until completion or confirmed worker loss. Worker loss
after
completed-result admission fails the task and preserves cleanup rather
than
redispatching potentially partly published targets. Missing local prefix
roots
are idempotent no-ops; other deletion failures remain retryable.

## Validation

Latest base synchronization: merged `master` at `b49b1e900b`. The only
textual
conflict was generated `data_coord.pb.go`; it was regenerated in the
development
container with `make generated-proto-without-cpp`. The other
PR-added/deleted
content is unchanged relative to the new base. Protobuf packages
compile, and
checks of field numbers and wire round trips preserve both upstream
compaction
`fail_status` and the PR's manifest/copy fields.

Targeted DataCoord/session tests on this merged revision could not
compile against
the existing local native output: it predates upstream
`create_token_stream`,
`ReadNext`, and `AddCColumnSplit` C API changes. These tests require a
refreshed
native build; no passing DataCoord runtime result is claimed for this
merge.
The focused runtime and lint results below apply to the pre-merge
revision.


Focused tests passed in the Milvus development container
`milvusdb/milvus-env:ubuntu22.04-20260714-c135601`, with the Conan cache
mounted and
`-tags dynamic,test -gcflags="all=-N -l" -count=1`:

- DataCoord copy task and cleanup lifecycle, Dropped recovery, and
publication/GC
  interleaving regressions: passed (13.570s).
- Existing copy inspector/checker/meta, manifest/reload and affected
dropped/index
  GC regressions: passed (16.084s).
- DataCoord session capability/compatibility and DataNode importv2
copy/manifest
  tests: passed (5.547s and 5.672s).
- Read-only Go formatting check and `git diff --check`: passed.
- Incremental repository-configured lint over the publication diff in
DataCoord,
  DataNode and packed storage packages: passed (0 issues).

These are focused unit and deterministic failure/interleaving tests.
Full CI,
real-cluster snapshot restore/QueryNode recovery and the race detector
were not
run for this update. A result installation already in progress can still
race an
external task-failure transition; the cleanup lock does not serialize
that older
state transition. The cleanup plan cannot recover unrecorded BuildIDs
from tasks
dispatched before the plan was introduced. Partition-level LOB cleanup
remains
owned by the existing orphan collector.

Turning publication off is supported, but it does not make
manifest-resident
metadata compatible with pre-feature DataCoord binaries. All potential
DataCoord
leaders must support manifest recovery and GC before activation.

## Known concurrency limitations (not fixed by this PR)

The segment manifest commit framework serializes its participating
writers,
including L0 batches. Two producers still generate revisions outside
that
boundary. Their limitations are tracked separately:

**Spark backfill on an ordinary StorageV3 collection — #53328.** Spark
can write
v11 = v10 + a backfilled column group while DataCoord still points to
v10. If an
index completion then publishes v12 = v10 + its index entry, the new
column group
is absent from v12. When backfill pre-validation passed before that
index commit,
the later `BatchUpdateManifest` ACK skips v11 as an older version and
`CommitBackfillResult` can nevertheless count the segment as committed.
The issue
tracks the exact pre-validation-to-ACK interleaving, final manifest
contents and
per-segment result correctness.

**External collection refresh patching an existing segment — #53329.**
Consider
unchanged external Parquet rows: refresh adds the mapping for `score`,
while an
index on existing field `id` completes. The DataNode patches the
manifest version
dispatched to it. If the index publishes v11 first, a refresh v12 built
from old
v10 can contain `score` but omit the index; DataCoord accepts v12
without checking
that input base. In the opposite order, an unadopted refresh v11 can be
overtaken
by index v12 lacking `score`, and the job treats v11 as already applied
merely
because v12 is newer. The issue covers both index recovery metadata loss
and a
successful refresh whose new column mapping is absent. This path applies
refresh
job results directly; it does not use `CommitBackfillResult` or the
batch ACK.

Until these issues are fixed, neither Spark backfill generation/adoption
nor an
existing-segment external refresh patch should overlap manifest commits
on that
same segment. The restriction covers base selection and revision
generation
through catalog publication; locking only the final adoption does not
close it.
These are source-derived failure sequences; deterministic concurrency
tests and
restart verification remain part of the respective issues' acceptance
criteria.

internal: url, Read the SCP-like form the way Git does The SCP-like grammar carried two rules canonical Git has never had. It read a leading run of one to five digits closed by a second colon as a TCP port, and it had no notion of a bracketed host at all. Git splits this form in parse_connect_url: the host ends at the first colon at or after the literal that host_end finds, and everything past that colon is the path. A port cannot appear, because get_host_and_port — the only place one is ever read — runs on the host half alone, and once the brackets are unwrapped that half holds no colon.

Reading a port where Git reads a path meant connecting somewhere Git
would not: `git@host:22:007/bond` dialled port 22 and asked for
`007/bond`, where Git asks the host for the path `22:007/bond` over the
default port. And with no bracket rule the host stopped at the first
colon whatever surrounded it, so `[fe80::1]:repo.git` parsed as host
`[fe80` with path `:1]:repo.git`, leaving no way to write an IPv6
address in this form. The host now keeps its brackets, which is what
net/url wants in URL.Host, what Hostname() unwraps for the transport,
and what has to be written back out for a rebuilt URL — a submodule
URL resolved against an SCP-like origin — to parse the same way again.

This breaks anyone relying on the port group. Any endpoint whose path
begins with one to five digits and a colon is now read as Git reads it:
host and default port, with those digits at the front of the path.
FindScpLikeComponents returns no port, and an endpoint that really does
mean a port has to be spelled as a URL, `ssh://git@host:22/path`, which
is what Git requires of it too.

The regexp in the tests is now the grammar go-git intends rather than
the one it inherited, and the sweeps, the named rules and the
differential fuzz target hold the scanners to it unchanged. Where
go-git stays deliberately stricter is recorded there: it still rejects
whitespace, and it does not copy Git's habit of dropping text written
between a `]` and the colon after it.

```text
input_ids:[8,4096];attention_mask:[8,4096]
```

ORT validates the configured graph-input shapes before cloning, applies
them to a disposable shadow graph, runs recursive shape inference, and
captures concrete intermediate `NodeArg` shapes without changing runtime
input constraints or executable-graph metadata.

The resolved shapes are consumed at:

- **Level 1:** CUDA `MatMulNBits` workspace estimation during
`GetCapability()`.
- **Level 2:** `DeclareWorkspaceRequirements()` on constructed kernels
during `FinalizeSessionState()`.

Static graph shapes remain usable at Level 2 without configuring an
override. Nodes whose inputs remain unresolved retain the existing
dynamic allocation/estimation fallback.

The shadow workflow:

- Shares existing initializer `OrtValue`s instead of copying large
weights.
- Preserves model-local functions and dynamically generated schemas.
- Captures main-graph and control-flow-subgraph shapes under separate
graph identities.
- Matches source and shadow control-flow nodes by stable identity
instead of topological position.
- Reuses results when the graph is unchanged and rebuilds them after
layout, fusion, or partitioning mutations.
- Converts shadow-model construction and resolution exceptions to
`Status`.

Invalid overrides fail with explicit errors, including unknown inputs,
rank mismatches, static-dimension conflicts, inconsistent symbolic
dimensions, empty entries, and malformed dimension lists. Minimal builds
warn and ignore the option rather than failing session initialization.

The inferred downstream shapes are estimation hints, not guaranteed
upper bounds: operator shape transformations are not necessarily
monotonic. Future preallocation must retain runtime bounds checks and
allocation fallbacks.

Level-2 declarations are currently observational. Workspace offset
planning and preallocation remain follow-up work.

### Motivation and Context

Dynamic transformer models commonly retain symbolic batch and sequence
dimensions, preventing workspace requirements from being calculated
before execution.

Deployment shape hints make partition-time budgeting and post-kernel
workspace declaration possible while preserving dynamic runtime
behavior. The isolated shadow graph prevents optimizers and runtime
validation from treating those hints as the model's static shape
contract.

This is part of the constrained-environment memory roadmap tracked by
#29775 and documented in
`docs/annotated_partitioning/future_directions_constrained_env.md`.

Kernels that do not implement `DeclareWorkspaceRequirements()` retain
the default no-op and continue using their existing scratch-allocation
path.

- Added coverage for parsing, malformed separators, zero extents, shape
propagation, canonical-graph isolation, invalid overrides, and stable

chore(release): Avoid edge case race conditions during Release prep and push (#3755)

# Change Summary

Protect the release window from changelog gaps.

The release process previously rendered the changelog at Prepare Release
time but created tags from the current `main` tip later. A pull request
merged during that window could therefore be included in the release
tags without appearing in that release's changelog.

This change closes the gap at three points:

1. **Before and after opening the release PR:** Prepare Release records
its starting `main` commit and verifies that the merge queue is empty
and `main` has not moved. If the first check fails, no PR is opened. If
the second check fails, the release PR remains open to freeze merges and
Prepare Release must be rerun to update it from the latest `main`.
2. **While the release PR is open:** The required `changelog` check
rejects every other pull request and merge-group entry. The release PR

that PR's merge commit rather than the current `main` tip.

geotiff: read_vrt(chunks=) builds a lazy dask graph (#1822)

* geotiff: build lazy dask graph for read_vrt(chunks=) (closes #1814)

Before this change, read_vrt(chunks=...) materialised the full VRT
mosaic on host RAM and then wrapped the resulting numpy array via
.chunk(). chunks= gave no memory protection, and gpu=True + chunks=
still assembled the entire mosaic on the CPU before moving to the
device.

The chunked path now parses the VRT XML once up front, builds one
dask.delayed per destination chunk window, and assembles them via
from_delayed + da.concatenate. Each task calls the existing VRT
internal reader with its own window= so only the sources intersecting
that window are decoded. With gpu=True each block calls cupy.asarray
before returning, so the dask array is dask-on-cupy from the start.

A task-count cap (50,000, matching read_geotiff_dask) refuses chunk
grids that would build a scheduler-busting graph and suggests a
larger chunks= value.

attrs['vrt_holes'] is not populated for chunked reads; the
GeoTIFFFallbackWarning still fires from each worker.

* geotiff: propagate vrt_holes and gate float64 promotion on chunked path (#1822 review)

Address Copilot review comments on PR #1822:

(c) The eager read_vrt populates attrs['vrt_holes'] as the machine-readable
partial-mosaic detection contract from #1734. The chunked path silently
omitted it. Populate the attr from a parse-time os.path.exists sweep over
every source referenced by the parsed VRT so callers switching from eager
to chunked keep the contract. The check is a static approximation that
catches the dominant missing-file case; codec-error holes still surface
as per-task GeoTIFFFallbackWarning.

(d) Document the static "any band declares nodata?" promotion check as
an explicit approximation of the eager path's runtime mask.any(). The
gate was already correct (no promotion when no band declares nodata) but
the surrounding comment did not call out the parse-time-vs-runtime
trade-off. Add a regression test pinning the no-nodata uint16 case to
the source dtype.

Defer the duplicated eager logic and N+1 VRT-XML re-parse via tracking
issue #1825; TODO markers reference that issue at both call sites.

* geotiff: per-tile dim check uses default cap, not caller budget (#1823)

PR #1803 forwarded the caller's max_pixels to read_to_array inside
read_vrt's source loop so a tiny VRT output cannot force a huge source
decode (#1796). The output-window check at the source read enforces that
correctly. A separate per-tile dimension check at the same call sites
also consumed the caller's max_pixels, so a caller setting max_pixels as
an output budget (e.g. 10_000) failed the per-tile sanity check on any
normal source whose default tile size is 256x256 (= 65_536 pixels).

Use MAX_PIXELS_DEFAULT for the per-tile dim check at the two call sites
in _read_tiles (local) and _read_tiles_cog_http (HTTP). The output-window
check at the same functions continues to enforce the user-supplied
max_pixels, preserving the #1796 protection.

* geotiff: clear _mmap_cache before unlink in #1814 hole test

The Windows 3.14 CI job failed with WinError 32 when the test tried
to unlink a tile referenced by the VRT: write_vrt() opens each tile
via _FileSource to read its header, and _FileSource.close() only
decrements the refcount in the shared _mmap_cache -- the mmap and
file handle remain idle in the cache. POSIX allows unlink of an
mmap'd file; Windows does not.

Call _mmap_cache.clear() (the cache's existing test helper, which
drops idle entries) immediately before os.unlink. Linux/macOS are
unaffected.

rust cli: Optimize remote summary fetch (#1666) ### Summary When opening a remote MCAP (`info`, `cat`, `list`, `get`, …), the Rust CLI previously made three sequential reads before touching any data: a range-support probe, a footer read, and a summary-section read. This collapses the common case to a **single range request** for the final 256 KiB of the file. That one request: - proves range support, - discovers the file size via `Content-Range`, and - in the overwhelmingly common case already contains the footer **and** the entire summary + summary-offset section. If the summary is larger than the tail, exactly one additional bounded request back-fills the missing prefix. If the server doesn't honor ranges at all, behavior is unchanged (fall back to scan/download, gated by `--allow-remote-scan`). ### Details - New `REMOTE_SUMMARY_TAIL_BYTES = 256 KiB` constant (well under the existing 16 MiB summary cap). - `RemoteUrlKind` distinguishes suffix-capable cloud stores (`CloudSuffix`: S3/S3-compatible, GCS) from those that reject suffix ranges (`CloudNoSuffix`: Azure Blob, which `object_store` fails fast for). HTTP and S3/GCS use a single `GetRange::Suffix` request; Azure uses `HEAD` + bounded tail. - `RemoteRangeReader::open` prefetches the tail; `read_summary_from_remote` parses footer + summary from it, back-filling only when the summary spills before the tail. - **HTTP servers that honor bounded ranges but reject suffix ranges** (either ignoring the suffix → `200`, or rejecting it → `416`) are handled: the suffix attempt falls back to a bounded `bytes=0-0` probe (which confirms range support and yields the size via `Content-Range`), then reads a bounded tail. Only if the bounded probe also shows no range support do we fall back to scan. This avoids regressing servers that previously opened fine, and avoids the misleading "does not support range requests" error / forced full download. - Per-store request counts (common case): HTTP and S3/GCS **3 → 1**; suffix-rejecting HTTP **3 → 3** (suffix + bounded probe + bounded tail, same as before this PR); Azure **3 → 2**. - A server that ignores `Range` and returns `200` with the full body is rejected by `object_store` at the response-header stage, so we fall back **without reading the body** — no risk of downloading a multi-GB file during discovery. ### Walkthrough End-to-end `mcap info` against logging HTTP servers (real 59 KB / 40-chunk MCAP): Suffix-capable server — summary discovery in **1** request (was 3): ``` GET Range=bytes=-262144 # suffix tail: range proof + size + footer + whole summary ``` [remote_summary_request_comparison.txt](https://cursor.com/agents/bc-fb02329b-90b3-46ef-80d7-455511ee13de/artifacts?path=%2Fopt%2Fcursor%2Fartifacts%2Fremote_summary_request_comparison.txt) Bounded-only server (rejects `bytes=-N` with `416`) — still opens via the index, no scan: ``` GET Range=bytes=-262144 -> 416 # suffix rejected GET Range=bytes=0-0 -> 206 # bounded probe: range support + size GET Range=bytes=0-59307 -> 206 # bounded tail ``` [bounded_only_server_recovery.txt](https://cursor.com/agents/bc-fb02329b-90b3-46ef-80d7-455511ee13de/artifacts?path=%2Fopt%2Fcursor%2Fartifacts%2Fbounded_only_server_recovery.txt) ### Review items addressed - **Bounded-but-not-suffix HTTP regression** — fixed via the bounded-probe fallback above. - **Test coverage for that case** — added a `bounded-only` mode to the test HTTP server (honors `bytes=S-E`, rejects `bytes=-N` with `416`) and a test asserting the file opens without a scan in exactly 3 requests. - **Tail invariant** — added a `debug_assert_eq!` in `read_summary_from_remote` documenting that the prefetched tail ends exactly at EOF. ### Testing - `cargo test -p mcap-cli` — 249 passed (5 new tests: tail-contains-summary fast path, back-fill, suffix-capability classification, single-request assertion, and bounded-only recovery). - `cargo clippy -p mcap-cli --all-targets -- --no-deps -D warnings` — clean. - `cargo fmt -p mcap-cli -- --check` — clean. - Manual end-to-end `mcap info` against suffix-capable, suffix-rejecting (416), and range-ignoring (200) servers (see walkthrough). [Compile] Make `lock_()` and other `_as_context_manager` ops compile-safe

The ``_as_context_manager`` decorator (used by ``lock_``/``unlock_``,
``to_module``, ``transpose``, ``flatten``, etc.) wrote a
``weakref.ref(self)`` into ``_last_op`` so the corresponding ``__exit__``
could call the inverse op. Under ``torch.compile`` that weakref becomes
a ``WeakRefVariable`` that Dynamo cannot reconstruct when the holding
TD flows out of the compiled region, which forced callers to defensively
call ``clear_refs_for_compile_()`` (and previously emitted a strong
warning around ``lock_`` itself).

Use a strong-ref closure (``_strong_ref(obj)`` returning ``lambda: obj``)
in place of ``weakref.ref`` when ``is_compiling()``. The closure is a
plain Python callable Dynamo can handle, and it's safe because the
compiled graph is transient: the closure is dropped as soon as the
outer call ends, so no real lifecycle cycle can form.

Also:

- Add ``_last_op = None`` as a class-level default on ``TensorDictBase``
  so ``__enter__`` can always read it (the compile path no longer writes
  it on every decorated call).
- Update the user-facing ``lock_`` warning to describe the real
  remaining caveat under compile: the parent/child unlock invariant is
  not enforced, the previous weakref-reconstruction failure is gone.

Adds a regression test asserting that a TD locked inside a compiled
function does not leak a real ``weakref.ref`` into ``_last_op``, and
that the strong-ref closure resolves back to the same TD.

Implements SDK-435: expands `consolidate_entity_descriptions_pipeline`
into the three-stage rewrite described in the ticket.

1. **Entity descriptions** — full rewrite from edges and `edge_text`,
bounded LLM concurrency.
2. **Type descriptions** — each `EntityType` description now summarizes
this graph's actual members (count, shared facts, comparisons only when
the data supports them) instead of just the type name, with batching +
merge for types with many members.
3. **`is_a` edge text** — each entity→type edge now carries a short
blend of that member against its type's summary, so the entity is
searchable as a member of its type.

`Entity.is_a` is widened to `(Edge, EntityType)` to carry that text, and
to support entities with more than one type.

A few real bugs surfaced while testing against an actual graph/LLM (not
just mocked tests) were fixed along the way: a missing-id crash on real
graph data, an LLM naming-threshold edge case now decided in code
instead of asked of the LLM, and entities with more than one type only
having the last type considered.

Configure udevd children-max for root-test

GHA runners occasionally experience I/O constraints during root-test
test execution. While concurrent tests rapidly allocate loopback
devices, background udev probing stalls. This quickly exhausts
systemd-udevd's default worker pool ceiling (20 children max), stalling
netlink uevent processing so device-mapper device nodes are never
created for subsequent dm-verity test execution.

Logging cgroups v2 pids.peak telemetry confirmed peak in-flight udev
workers accumulate to 325 during test execution. Raising the
children-max limit to 500 provides comfortable buffer room so udevd
freely spawns worker processes without entering event lockup or causing
test timeouts.

feat: add import profiler tool with dynamic loaded lines code volume … (#17467)

###  Overview
This PR introduces `profiler.py`, a zero-dependency, process-isolated
import profiling tool designed to benchmark Python SDK modules with
extreme precision and zero dynamic cache interference.

To evaluate authentic import initialization overhead without the
"observer effect", the profiler leverages a Master/Worker architecture.
The master orchestrator executes each benchmark iteration inside a
completely isolated, dynamically spawned subprocess. By bypassing
Python's `sys.modules` cache and sweeping disk-level `__pycache__`
directories, the tool guarantees a 100% authentic "cold-start"
evaluation every time.

### Key Telemetry Vectors & Features
- **Initialization Latency (ms):** Measured at high resolution natively,
securely omitting VM startup skew.
- **Physical Memory Deltas (RAM):** Employs a dual-strategy approach
tracking both internal block allocator shifts via `tracemalloc`
(cross-platform), and pure OS-level physical memory footprints via
`/proc/self/statm` deltas (Linux RSS) to catch heavy C/C++ backend
extensions like `protobuf`.
- **Deterministic Code Volume (LOC):** Tracks the physical delta of
`sys.modules` across the import window, traversing disk paths to
aggregate the exact number of physical Lines of Code (LOC) injected into
the interpreter.
- **CPU Pinning:** Binds worker processes to a single CPU core via
`taskset` on Linux to eliminate OS-level context-switching jitter across
iterations.
- **Diagnostic Tooling:** Supports one-off diagnostic tracing for
bottleneck discovery via `--trace` (`-X importtime`) and `--cprofile`.

*A comprehensive breakdown of the architecture, data pipeline, and trace
log analysis is documented in
[`scripts/import_profiler/documentation.md`](./scripts/import_profiler/documentation.md).*

[BugFix][Relax] Add structural_equal verification to subroutine cache lookup (#18962)

## Summary

- `SubroutineMixin._get_subroutine()` used `structural_hash` as the sole
cache key without `structural_equal` verification. If two different
`arg_sinfo` values produced the same 64-bit hash (collision), the cache
would return a previously compiled function with mismatched parameter
shapes, leading to silently incorrect compiled output.
- Changed the cache to store a list of `(arg_sinfo, result)` pairs per
hash bucket and verify with `structural_equal` on lookup, consistent
with the pattern in `block_builder.cc`.
- Added a security advisory document and regression test.

## Root Cause

The subroutine cache (`cls._gvar`) was keyed by
`(structural_hash(arg_sinfo), is_dataflow)`. A hash match was treated as
proof of structural equality, skipping the necessary `structural_equal`
check. This is a hash-only lookup anti-pattern — hash determines the
bucket, but equality must confirm the match.

For comparison, `block_builder.cc` correctly uses `StructuralHash` +
`StructuralEqual` together as the hash and equality functions for
`std::unordered_map`.

- [ ] New test `test_different_shapes_produce_distinct_subroutines`
passes — verifies that the same Module class with different input shapes

consistent with how prior plugin behavior changes are versioned.

fix(engine): apply ancestor transforms through a read-resource parent (#24689)

## Summary

Resource transforms declared on an ancestor component were silently not
applied to a custom resource when the resource's parent chain passed
through a read (`.get()`-style) resource. The engine collects the
transforms to run on a resource by walking up the parent chain via
`rm.parents` (a URN→parent URN map), but that map was populated only in
the `RegisterResource` path — `ReadResource` never recorded a `parent`
entry for the resource it creates. When the ancestor walk reached a read
resource it found no entry and stopped early, dropping every transform
declared on components above the read resource.

This fixes `ReadResource` in `pkg/resource/deploy/source_eval.go` to
record `rm.parents[urn] = parent` for the resource it creates, mirroring
what `RegisterResource` already does. A read resource has no transforms
of its own (there's no `Transforms` field on `ReadResourceRequest`), so
`rm.resourceTransforms` is intentionally left untouched for it — only
the parent-chain link needed for the walk to continue.

[FLINK-31931][runtime-web] Stop polling a TaskManager once it is gone

The TaskManager status and metrics views re-requested the TaskManager detail
on every refresh tick, so a TaskManager that had been lost kept generating
failing /taskmanagers/<id> requests indefinitely. loadManager also swallowed
every error, hiding the not-found case from callers.

Let loadManager propagate errors and share a small poll helper that stops
once the backend reports the TaskManager is gone (404), while transient
errors keep retrying. The status view then shows a "no longer available"
notice instead of an endless skeleton, and the metrics cards are hidden
instead of rendering blank tables.

The global HTTP interceptor turns every error body into a persistent
"Server Response Message" notification, which for the now-expected 404 meant
a full server stack trace popping up next to the notice. loadManager marks
its request with an EXPECTED_NOT_FOUND HttpContext token and the interceptor
skips the notification for a 404 on such a request; every other error is
still surfaced as before.

fix: add hSetNX to Redis transaction interface (#248)

## Summary

Adds `hSetNX` to the Redis transaction interface (`TxClientLike`) and
both transaction class implementations. The method exists in the
non-transaction `RedisClient` but was missing from transactions.

## Why this matters

[#184](https://github.com/reddit/devvit/issues/184) reports that
`hSetNX` is unavailable in transactions. The `TxClientLike` type has
`hSet`, `hGet`, `hMGet`, `hGetAll`, `hDel`, `hScan`, `hKeys`, `hIncrBy`,
and `hLen` but not `hSetNX`. This makes it impossible to use atomic

Remove redundant Atomic wrapper and fix shared-prefix extraction in regex reduction (#126114)

Two small regex tree reduction improvements found during analysis of
17,434 real-world patterns from `Regex_RealWorldPatterns.json`
(#126104):

**1. Remove redundant Atomic wrapper from non-backtrackable nodes**

`ReduceAtomic()` already unwraps `Atomic` from `Empty`/`Nothing`
children, but not from `One`/`Notone`/`Set`/`Multi` children that also
inherently cannot backtrack. These arise when the user writes `(?>...)`
wrapping content that reduces to a single fixed-length match, e.g.
`(?>\u591C[\u665A\u91CC\u95F4])`. The Atomic wrapper adds unnecessary
save/restore scaffolding. Affects 383 patterns (2.2%).

No measurable perf impact (JIT already eliminates the dead code), but
produces a cleaner tree.

**2. Fix `ExtractCommonPrefixText` to continue past non-text branches**

The method bails out of the entire alternation when
`FindBranchOneOrMultiStart()` returns null for any branch. This prevents
factoring later consecutive text branches that share a prefix. For
example in `[^#;]|\\#|\\;`, the Set branch causes early return, so
branches `\\#` and `\\;` (which share prefix `\`) are never factored.

Changed `return alternation` to `continue` so the outer loop advances
past non-text branches. The inner loop and singleton-run check already
handle all edge cases correctly. Affects 1,090 patterns (6.3%), though
most are 2-branch cases with negligible perf benefit. ~50 patterns with
4+ shared branches see modest improvement from enabling switch dispatch.

[http-client-csharp] Fix trailing path separator for optional path parameter (#11096)

## Problem

When a route ends with an **optional** path parameter, the `/` separator
preceding that segment was emitted unconditionally, leaving a dangling
trailing slash when the value is null.

For example, `/certificates/{certificate-name}/{certificate-version}`
(with `certificate-version` optional) generated:

```csharp
uri.AppendPath(certificateName, true);
uri.AppendPath("/", false);            // emitted unconditionally
if ((certificateVersion != null))
{
    uri.AppendPath(certificateVersion, true);
}
```

So when `certificateVersion` is null the wire URL becomes
`/certificates/{name}/` instead of `/certificates/{name}`. Services
(e.g. Key Vault) and recorded test cassettes expect no trailing slash.

The existing `shouldPrependWithPathSeparator` logic only handled the
case where the preceding literal does *not* end in `/`; it missed the
case where the separator had already been written unconditionally.

## Fix

In `RestClientProvider.AddUriSegments`, when the upcoming path parameter
is optional and the preceding literal ends with `/`, defer that trailing
`/` so it is written together with the parameter value inside the null
check:

```csharp
uri.AppendPath(certificateName, true);
if ((certificateVersion != null))
{
    uri.AppendPath("/", false);
    uri.AppendPath(certificateVersion, true);
}
```

Required path parameters are unaffected.

## Tests

- Added `TestBuildCreateRequestMethodWithOptionalPathParameter` (+
golden file) covering the trailing optional-segment case.
- Updated two `ServerTemplate*` tests that relied on the test factory's
default `isRequired: false` for what were intended to be normal required
path parameters.
- Full `Microsoft.TypeSpec.Generator.ClientModel` suite passes (1440
tests).

[win32] Fix collapsed tab stops at fractional zoom levels

TextLayout.setTabs() takes tab stops in points, but computeRuns()
compared them in pixels against a pen position summed from raw glyph
advances. At zoom levels that are not a multiple of 100 the round trip
can put a stop one pixel past a pen sitting exactly on it, so the tab

spaces rounded to points. Stops beyond the first are multiples of that
rounded value and drift further off the grid of spaces, so a tab after

- implement setDefaultTabWidth() on win32, as cocoa does since bug

Refactors the `CdnDownloadStrategy` to use dedicated helper methods for directory creation and file extraction. This improves readability and maintainability of the archive processing logic.

* fix(cdn-download): prevent path traversal in zip extraction

Add validation to the `extractEntry` function to prevent path traversal vulnerabilities during the extraction of zip archives. The target path is now resolved against the base directory of the extraction to ensure it remains within the intended scope.
This change enhances security by ensuring that malicious zip archives cannot write files outside of their designated extraction directory.
The `baseDir` option is now passed to `extractEntry` and used to construct a safe target path.

* fix(plugin-system): improve error handling and stream management in cdn download

This commit addresses several issues in the `CdnDownloadStrategy` related to error handling and stream management during plugin downloads.
Key changes:
- **Robust Error Logging:** Error messages for directory creation and file extraction now include the full error stack or message for better debugging. They also explicitly convert non-Error objects to strings.
- **Stream Pipeline for Extraction:** The `entry.pipe(writeStream)` and `finished(writeStream)` combination has been replaced with `pipeline(entry, writeStream)`. This provides more reliable error propagation and ensures streams are properly cleaned up.
- **Resource Cleanup on Error:** In the `extractFile` method, if an error occurs during file extraction, the `entry` and `writeStream` are explicitly destroyed to release resources.
- **Incomplete File Removal:** If an error occurs during file extraction, any partially created target file is now removed to prevent leaving incomplete artifacts. This handles potential `ENOENT` errors gracefully.
- **Throwing Errors:** Errors are now consistently re-thrown after cleanup, ensuring that the calling code is aware of and can handle extraction failures.

* fix(cdn-download): re-throw stream write errors

The previous implementation of `CdnDownloadStrategy` caught stream write errors and autodrained the entry. This masked the underlying error and prevented `Promise.all` from rejecting, leading to silent failures when downloading plugin files.
This change re-throws the caught error. This ensures that any failure during the file writing process is propagated up to `Promise.all`, allowing the overall download operation to fail gracefully and be reported to the user.

* fix: Rethrowing here propagates the error, but the unzipper entry stream is no longer drained/destroyed on failure. A write error can leave the entry unread and stall the unzip parse. Drain (or destroy) the entry before rethrowing.

* fix(mobile): harden TimeUI fallback recovery (call fina(), de-dupe popovers)

Devin Review correctly flagged that the safety-net path in
MobileTimeUIToggle.handleClick was producing a partially-broken TimeUI
when it fired:

- TimeUI.init() unconditionally appends a new #timeUIPlayPopover_global
  to <body>, so a second init() left two elements with the same id.
- TimeUI.init() alone does not wire up date pickers or per-button click
  handlers — that's TimeUI.fina()'s job. Without fina(), the recovered
  TimeUI rendered visually but Play / Previous / Next / Fit / Follow /
  Present / Expand were all dead.

Before re-initializing, remove the stale #timeUIPlayPopover_global and
#timeUIQuickSelectPopover_global divs to avoid duplicate ids. After the
new #timeUI is moved into #tools, call TimeUI.fina() to populate the
date pickers, attach the button click handlers, build the histogram,
and populate the expanded mobile rows.

Some delegated body/document handlers in attachEvents() will still be
duplicated on this path; that is acceptable for a degraded recovery
that should never run in practice now that the primary rescues in
ToolController_.makeTool() and Coordinates.js cover all known paths.

* fix: serialize concurrent layer reloads and stop mutating layer.url

Concurrent mmgisAPI.reloadLayer() calls for the same layer were
silently dropped by the _layersBeingMade guard, and reloadLayer
mutated layer.url in-place during async work — causing a race where

permanently corrupt the {starttime}/{endtime} template placeholders.

  dropping it with a 'Cannot make layer' warning.

  for this layer via setTimeout 0.
- TimeControl.reloadTimeLayers: become async and await Promise.all
  of every per-layer reload; remove the setTimeout(500) workaround
  around active-feature restoration and follow-pan logic.

* fix: thread resolvedUrl through makeLayer/captureVector instead of mutating layer.url

The previous fix in Map_.refreshLayer temporarily swapped
`layerObj.url = resolvedUrl` during the `await makeLayer` call and
restored it in a finally block. Since `layerObj` is the shared
`L_.layers.data[name]` object, any concurrent code reading
`layer.url` during that async window could observe the resolved URL
instead of the template. Most importantly, a second
`TimeControl.reloadLayer()` call would then capture the resolved
URL as its 'template' and corrupt the placeholders for every
subsequent reload.

Surfaced by tests/e2e/time/concurrent-layer-reload.spec.js Test 5,
which after Promise.all of two reloads observed
`layer.url ==='geodatasets:...?from=...&to=...'` instead of the
expected `{starttime}/{endtime}` template.

`Map_.refreshLayer` -> `makeLayer` -> `makeVectorLayer` ->
`captureVector` (via options.resolvedUrl). `captureVector` uses
`options.resolvedUrl` when provided and skips the
`{starttime}`/`{endtime}`/`{customtime.*}` regex replacement
(which TimeControl.reloadLayer already performed). `layer.url` is
NEVER mutated for the duration of the async operation, so the
template is preserved across overlapping reloads.

This also fully resolves the Devin Review #4 finding which flagged
the temporary URL swap as reintroducing the same race the PR was
meant to fix.

* fix: always run time-placeholder replacement in captureVector (idempotent)

The previous fix gated captureVector's time-placeholder replacement
block on `!hasResolvedUrl`, on the assumption that any caller passing
options.resolvedUrl had already done the replacement.

That assumption only holds for time.type === 'global' / 'requery' /
forceRequery. For other time types that still flow through
Map_.refreshLayer into captureVector (most importantly
time.type === 'local' with endProp == null per TimeControl.js:276-287),

literal {starttime}/{endtime}/{time} placeholders. The fetch then goes
out with unreplaced placeholders.

reading the source from `layerUrl` (which is already either
options.resolvedUrl or layerObj.url per the choice above). The
.replace(/{starttime}/g, ...) chain is idempotent on URLs that have
already been resolved — the regexes simply don't match — so the
correct path is restored without re-introducing the mutate-in-place
bug fcba8101 fixed.

* fix(makeLayer): wrap dispatch in try/finally so lock + queue drain always run

Address Devin Review finding: a thrown exception from any layer-type
builder (makeVectorLayer, makeVelocityLayer, etc.) inside makeLayer's
switch statement previously left lockRegistry[layerName] set to true
and skipped the queue drain entirely, since the release statement and
queue-drain block both lived AFTER the awaited dispatch.

Effect of the bug: any subsequent refreshLayer call for that layer
would queue against a permanently-locked entry that never drains.
The new queue mechanism inherits this pre-existing issue and makes
the failure mode worse — silent accumulation in _layerReloadQueue
instead of a visible 'Cannot make layer' warning.

Additional concern: the outer 'new Promise(async (resolve, reject) =>
{...})' is the async-executor anti-pattern. A throw inside the async
executor escapes to the unhandled-rejection handler instead of
rejecting the outer Promise — so the caller's 'await makeLayer(...)'
would hang indefinitely, compounding the lock-leak symptom.

Fix:
  - Wrap the type-dispatch switch + Filtering.updateGeoJSON/
    triggerFilter calls in a try/catch/finally.
  - catch logs the error and tracks success via 'madeSuccessfully'.
  - finally runs unconditionally: lockRegistry[layerName] = false,
    drain L_._layerReloadQueue[layerObj.name] if present, then
    resolve(madeSuccessfully). This ensures the lock release and
    queue drain happen regardless of whether the inner builder
    threw or completed normally.

Test (concurrent-layer-reload.spec.js):
  Added probe-style test '_layersBeingMade lock is released after
  single and concurrent reloads' that asserts the lock invariant:
    1. After mmgisAPI.reloadLayer() resolves +
       a 100ms drain window, _layersBeingMade[key] is false.
    2. After 5 concurrent mmgisAPI.reloadLayer() calls resolve +
       a 1000ms drain window, _layersBeingMade[key] is false.
    3. _layerReloadQueue is empty afterwards (otherwise a future
       reload would mistakenly trigger an immediate drain instead
       of doing its own work).

  This is a positive-invariant test — it catches accidental lock
  retention even without force-triggering exceptions, which would
  require monkey-patching webpack-internal module references that
  aren't exposed on window.

Per user direction, NOT addressing Devin Review's separate finding
about the reloadTimeLayers sync->async breaking change at this
time (no version bump requested).
